items.title: Vercel Schedules (public beta): agents and apps can create, change, or cancel schedules through code -- no redeploy, no DB-plus-polling-job
items.summary: Static schedules still live in vercel.json and sync on deploy. The new part is dynamic schedules: an agent calls the JS SDK, CLI, or API at runtime to create a one-time or recurring schedule, backed by Vercel Queues, with no database table or cron-polling loop of your own. You can test scheduled work on Preview deployments before it runs in production.
items.why: This removes a whole category of boilerplate -- the database-plus-polling-job pattern -- for any agent that needs to act later instead of right now.

items.title: Google: coding agents get measurably distracted by stale TODO/FIXME comments -- unprompted detours cost 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, 105% more wait time
items.summary: Across hundreds of millions of agent steps, Google engineers found 13% of file-reading sessions exposed the agent to an inline TODO(bug/...) or FIXME(bug/...) reference. The agent ignored it 94% of the time, but in the other 6% it often chased the bug unprompted, and 41% of those detours chased tickets that were already closed. A fixed-effects regression put the cost of an unprompted detour at 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session (all p<0.0001). Their fix: an internal TODO-cleaner agent that cross-checks bug and file history before proposing removal -- it has removed thousands of stale references over 6 months with over 95% human-reviewer acceptance.
items.why: Stale comments and dead references are a direct, measurable tax on your own agents' steps and tokens, not just an annoyance for human readers -- and it's something you can actually scan for and clean up.
items.action: Grep your own repo for TODO/FIXME comments referencing closed or ancient tickets, and see how many your coding agent would plausibly wander into on an unrelated task.

items.title: Simon Willison: hide your agent-written PR description behind a collapsed <details><summary> tag, with a one-line human summary on top
items.summary: GitHub Markdown renders <details><summary> as a collapsed heading you can click to expand, and it works directly in PR descriptions and issue comments. Willison now writes one short, human-judged opening line himself, then wraps the full agent-written essay underneath in a <details> block labeled with the model name, e.g. 'Claude Opus 5.5 Medium.' Nothing is lost -- reviewers just aren't confronted with paragraphs of agent prose by default.
items.why: It's a 30-second habit that fixes the exact thing that makes reviewers tune out agent-generated PRs, without losing any of the detail the agent wrote.
items.action: On your next Claude Code or Codex PR, write one human sentence as the opener and wrap the agent's full description in <details><summary>Model name</summary>...</details> underneath.

items.title: I Let Agents Refactor My Codebase for 3 Weeks. Then I Read the Code. -- Keiji Kanazawa, Microsoft
items.summary: Three weeks into letting coding agents refactor his personal research agent, a bad digest sent Kanazawa looking for a trace -- and he found the 'agent' was still a deterministic workflow wearing agent language: skills with no SKILL.md, different architectural concepts that were secretly aliases for the same thing, a daily reflection job quietly producing empty reports. He rebuilt around an explicit agent runtime and goal rubrics, comparing four agent frameworks, then caught one of his own evaluation rubrics overfitting when it failed on five other videos.
items.why: A concrete, slightly embarrassing story of approving agent plans without checking whether the implementation actually means what its labels promise -- plus a working pattern for catching it.

items.title: What the Top Companies Do Differently With AI Coding -- Martin Harrysson & Prakhar Dixit, McKinsey
items.summary: McKinsey's own data across large companies using AI coding agents: most report only modest gains, but the top 20-25% are now seeing 2x end-to-end improvements from the same tools. The standout point, echoed in the comments: the gap is operating model, not tooling -- once generation gets fast, the bottleneck moves to requirements and release, i.e. validation and deployment were always the hard part.
items.why: A quantified answer to 'why isn't my team seeing the gains everyone talks about' -- worth it specifically to check whether your team's bottleneck has quietly moved from writing code to reviewing and shipping it.
